content.text:
Done. `/app/answers.json` is written and valid, and the full budget of 40 runs was used.

**What I measured.** A fresh-data scaling law fits all unrepeated q=0 runs to 0.004 nats rms. Repetition follows a saturating effective-data curve with roughly 6.5 "useful" repeats, independent of N. Quality filtering acts as a per-token value multiplier of about 1.34 at q=0.6 and 1.22 at q=0.5, possibly decaying slowly with D. Seed noise is about 0.005 nats, so the team's note that filtering "buys nothing measurable" was wrong: on fresh data it helps clearly, but on the small ablation subset the extra epochs cancelled the gain.

**Answers.**

| id | answer | basis |
|---|---|---|
| q1 | 0.024 nats | 5 epochs on 4e10 tokens is worth about 1.55e11 effective tokens vs 2e11 |
| q2 | +0.014 nats | at q=0.5 the 10 epochs cost more than the token-value gain |
| q3 | A (q=0) | every filter level loses on the 4e10 snapshot |
| q4 | refuted | fresh-data gain at D=1e11 is only 0.017 to 0.035 nats, all fits below 0.050 |
| q5 | [-0.004, +0.038] | filtering helps slightly at 1e11 unique tokens, hurts at 2e10 |
| q6 | undetermined | sign of the q=0.6 effect flips across the 2e10 to 1e11 snapshot range |

**Caveat.** The q5 lower endpoint and the q6 verdict rest on a margin of a few thousandths of a nat at the 1e11 end of the snapshot range. Three of four candidate filter laws put filtering marginally ahead there, so I answered undetermined rather than refuted.
